newsitem.title: USA: Taiwan-N.Korea nuclear waste plan raises concerns.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan-N.Korea nuclear waste plan raises concerns.

text.p: The United States has raised concerns with Taiwan over a plan to ship low-level nuclear waste to North Korea for storage, a congressional panel was told on Wednesday.
Charles Kartman, an acting assistant secretary of state, called the issue "rather thorny" and indicated that Washington would prefer that Taiwan build its own nuclear storage facilities.

Representative Doug Bereuter, a Nebraska Republican and chairman of a House International Relations subcommittee, told Kartman he had passed on to the State Department South Korea's concerns about the preliminary plan and asked whether it signalled the start of a broader relationship between Taiwan and North Korea.
Kartman replied that Washington had discussed the issue with Taiwan authorities.
"We have raised with them enviromnental concerns, concerns over safety of shipping and storage," he said.

"We have discussed with them the standards that ought to be met with respect to the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) inspection and monitoring and we have also raised with them the concerns of other countries in the region which ought to be satisfied before proceeding," Kartman said.
He said it was impossible to say whether the plan indicated expanding ties between Taiwan and North Korea.
He said North Korea needed the hard currency offered by Taiwan, and Tawain needed storage for its nuclear waste.
"We would urge them to go elsewhere but nonetheless they have this need," he said.
Asked if he would urge Tawain to construct its own facilities, he said: "We would believe that that would be an appropriate solution."

In a statement Bereuter also voiced concern about continued food aid to North Korea by the United States and other countries, asking if it "merely supports a discredited and tottering regime that could not exist without external assistance."

Bereuter added: "Since the root problems of a totally inefficient state-run agricultural system are not being addressed, are we to assume that we will be asked to provide food assistance again and again and again."
He suggested the United States and international community "have a right to expect fundamental changes from this pariah state in return for our largesse."

Kartman defended the U.S. contribition of more than $18 million in emergency cash and food to North Korea -- including a $10 million in-kind contribition earlier this month -- as being in the tradition of providing assistance to people in need.
"The prospect of widespread hunger, or even famine this spring creates the possibility of unrest, dislocation of North Korean civilians in search of food and other difficulties," he said.

He said North Korean policy and decision-making were not expected to change significantly after the likely assumption by the country's leader Kim Jong-il of the titles of president and secretary-general of the Korean Workers' Party later this year.
